purpose: Evidence backbone for the MirrorMii launch survey. Every card starts from a sub-question (what it measures) and then picks a scenario (how it hides it). Founder direction 2026-09-29: first establish the sub-question, then the scenario.

rules.poles: poleA is the + pole for axes and the A tag for pairs; poleB is the - pole or the B tag. Evidence on a card follows the pole the chosen behavior implies, never the joke.
rules.targets: primary is what the sub-question exists to measure; secondary is a nearby signal a card writer may add only when the option's behavior itself implies it (library and skill rules still apply, e.g. T06 is capacity: tag only, never R2).

worlds.absurd: Impossible or magic (Genii's wish with a catch, impossible trades, animals, time magic, powers, cursed objects). Scored as would or believe. The option lines must name the real-world meaning so the choice maps.
worlds.unusual: Possible but rare (elevator with an ex, jury duty, an inheritance, a reality show, a wrong-number group chat). Scored as would.
worlds.everyday: Grounded; only for did-evidence formats. format: real (the last time), receipts (tap what's true), bet (Genii's bet / guilty or not).

rules.bans: No em dashes. Gender neutral (your partner, your parent, sibling). No health, body, diet, politics, religion, explicit sex or age references. Never cruel to a type of person. Every side costs something: no good-person answer.
rules.uniqueness: No seed setting repeats across the map; Genii wishes each carry a different catch.

subquestions.question: When closeness and freedom collide, which do you protect?
subquestions.poleA: Merges time and space with the person: shared evenings, one calendar, says yes to always together.
subquestions.poleB: Keeps a room, a night or a plan of their own even when very close.
subquestions.tension: Choosing closeness costs your own edges and quiet; choosing space costs the other person's sense of being chosen.

absurd.text: An enchanted red string ties you to your partner: you can never be more than a mile apart, forever, and it can only be cut today.

unusual.text: A reality show offers you and your closest person $50,000 to spend 30 days handcuffed together, or $20,000 each to spend them on opposite sides of the house.

everyday.text: The last evening you and your closest person were both free: how it actually got spent.

subquestions.notes: Absurd seed works because the ask is keep or cut the string; a card must offer a proud 'cut it' option so Me is not the cold answer.

subquestions.question: Does being close mean knowing everything, or trusting what you don't know?
subquestions.poleA: Tells the full story fast and expects the same back: moods, news, whereabouts.
subquestions.poleB: Keeps some rooms private and doesn't ask for theirs.
subquestions.tension: Full transparency costs privacy and the right to a bad day in peace; privacy costs reassurance and can read as hiding.

absurd.text: A cursed bracelet glows your exact mood to your partner all day; you can take it off, but it texts them that you did.

unusual.text: A brand offers you and your best friend a free week abroad if your phones mirror each other's screens the whole trip.

everyday.text: Your last big news, good or bad: how many hours passed before your closest person heard it.

subquestions.notes: Stay off phone passcodes here (that is T01); keep this about news and moods.

subquestions.question: When your people decide something together, do you go with the group or peel off?
subquestions.poleA: Goes along to stay one unit, even with doubts; the group's plan becomes theirs.
subquestions.poleB: Says 'you go, I'll catch you after' and follows their own plan.
subquestions.tension: Going along costs your own wants; peeling off costs your place in the story the group tells later.

absurd.text: Your whole friend group is offered seats on the first trip to Mars, all or nothing, and everyone but you has already said yes.

unusual.text: Your friend group's shared lottery ticket wins, and the vote is 5 to 1 to spend every cent on one group house; you're the 1.

everyday.text: The last group plan you didn't love: whether you went, or peeled off to do your own thing.

subquestions.notes: Mars reads as risk (L1) unless the card frames the pressure as the group vote, not space travel. Keep 'stay behind' options warm, never lonely.

subquestions.question: When the truth will hurt someone you like, do you say it now or protect them first?
subquestions.poleA: Says it plainly, today, before it gets worse.
subquestions.poleB: Cushions it, waits for a better moment, or lets them find out gently.
subquestions.tension: Saying it now can wound and cost the friendship; waiting can let them walk into something worse and makes you part of it.

absurd.text: A magic 8-ball that has never been wrong says your friend's crush will say no, and your friend is about to confess in front of everyone.

unusual.text: Your friend pitches to real investors tomorrow, and tonight you find the exact same product already sold online.

everyday.text: The last time someone asked 'be honest, what do you think?' and you didn't like it.

subquestions.notes: Keep the crush gender neutral. The friend's hope must be visible so the soft option stays charming.

subquestions.question: When someone crosses a line with you, do you name it or absorb it?
subquestions.poleA: Calls it out to their face, same day.
subquestions.poleB: Lets it pass, hints, or waits until it matters more.
subquestions.tension: Naming it risks a scene and the relationship; absorbing it costs you resentment and invites a repeat.

absurd.text: For one year: a hundred jellyfish as pets that each sting you a little every day, or three big spiders as opponents you face down once each.

unusual.text: Your team wins an award for the idea your coworker claimed as theirs, and you're both called on stage to accept it.

everyday.text: The last time a roommate, sibling or friend kept doing the one small thing that bugs you.

subquestions.notes: Founder's jellyfish seed maps weakly on its own. Frame it explicitly: many small stings you quietly live with (Soft) versus three fights, then done (Direct). Options must say that out loud.

subquestions.question: In a group, do you say what everyone is thinking, or keep the peace?
subquestions.poleA: Says it to the whole group, out loud.
subquestions.poleB: Keeps the room calm; handles it privately, later, or not at all.
subquestions.tension: Saying it can make you the villain and split the group; keeping the peace lets the problem run and makes you complicit.

absurd.text: Your friend group is stranded on a desert island and one friend keeps hogging the only hammock, every night, with a smile.

unusual.text: At a surprise party, the group previews the slideshow one friend made, and it roasts the guest of honor way too hard; it plays in ten minutes.

everyday.text: The last group chat where someone said something that landed badly and everyone went quiet.

subquestions.notes: Island risks a survival read; keep stakes social (the hammock), not food or safety.

subquestions.question: Do the old rituals feel like home, or like a costume?
subquestions.poleA: Keeps the holidays, milestones and rituals the way they have always been done.
subquestions.poleB: Remixes or skips them and builds their own.
subquestions.tension: Keeping the ritual can mean living someone else's script; skipping it can cost belonging and a hurt family.

absurd.text: Time magic: relive one childhood holiday exactly as it was, or skip every future holiday and get the days back to spend anywhere.

unusual.text: A surprise inheritance leaves you your grandparent's house, on one condition: you host the whole family's big yearly dinner there, every year.

everyday.text: The last big holiday: your family's usual way, or your own thing.

subquestions.notes: Never grade tradition as old-fashioned or skipping as disrespectful. No religion: say 'holiday', never name one.

subquestions.question: Should a home and a couple run the way it has always been done, or by a design you invent?
subquestions.poleA: Runs home roles, names and routines the way the family always did.
subquestions.poleB: Negotiates everything from zero: roles, names, routines.
subquestions.tension: The script is easy and familiar but may not fit; inventing fits better but means endless negotiation and raised eyebrows.

absurd.setting: robot set to your parents' home
absurd.text: A household robot arrives preprogrammed to run your future home exactly like your parents' did, down to who cooks and who pays; keep the settings or wipe it.

unusual.text: A mix-up on the lease lets you put your name, your partner's name, or a brand-new name you both invent on the door.

everyday.text: The last time you and someone you live with split chores: whose family's system won.

subquestions.notes: Gender neutral always: never imply who 'should' cook or pay. The name seed must work for any couple.

subquestions.question: When the family you came from and the person you chose both need you, whose claim comes first?
subquestions.poleA: The family you came from comes first; the old bond is the backbone.
subquestions.poleB: The family you are building comes first; the chosen bond is the new center.
subquestions.tension: Choosing the old family can make your partner feel second forever; choosing your partner can feel like leaving home for good.

absurd.text: Your parent and your partner fall into a river, you have one floatie, and they swim equally badly: who gets it first?

unusual.text: Your parent's big anniversary party and your partner's once-in-a-lifetime award dinner land on the same night, in different cities.

everyday.text: The last time your family's plans and your partner's plans collided, and which side you picked.

subquestions.notes: Founder's river seed. Keep it comic and rescuable (both get out; the ask is 'first'); never framed as death. Maps to R3 only if options name the bond (the family I came from / the one I'm building), else it is a pure loyalty poll. Mark privacy intimate.

subquestions.question: Would you trade a sure good thing for a shot at a great unknown?
subquestions.poleA: Keeps the good life they already have.
subquestions.poleB: Trades it for the unknown that might be better.
subquestions.tension: Keeping it risks a small life and a long 'what if'; trading it risks losing everything that already worked.

absurd.text: Genii offers to swap your whole life, home, job and friends, for a random new one in a random country, guaranteed 'at least as good', no previews.

unusual.text: A hotel guest you once gave directions to turns out to own an island resort and offers you the manager job, starting in three weeks.

everyday.text: The last time a sure option and a riskier, more exciting one were both on the table, and which you took.

subquestions.notes: Genii catch: no previews. Keep the current life described as good so Steady is not settling.

subquestions.question: When you can't see how it ends, do you step in or wait for more information?
subquestions.poleA: Waits, researches, needs a plan B before moving.
subquestions.poleB: Steps in blind and figures it out on the way.
subquestions.tension: Waiting can mean the door closes; stepping in blind can mean falling with no net.

absurd.text: A door appears in your hallway with a note: 'Somewhere wonderful. No coming back for a year. Closes tonight.'

unusual.text: You win a free trip where the destination is only announced once the plane doors close.

everyday.text: The last plan or trip you started without knowing how it would work out, or didn't start because of that.

subquestions.question: Do you keep a safety net, even when it holds you back?
subquestions.poleA: Keeps the backup: the day job, the cushion, the lease.
subquestions.poleB: Cuts it to go all in.
subquestions.tension: The net means half commitment and a slower start; no net means a real fall if it fails.

absurd.text: A letter in your own handwriting, dated ten years from now, says: 'Quit the safety net this month. Trust me.' No proof it's real.

unusual.text: You're on a game show and can walk away with $20,000, or risk it all on one final question about a topic you half know.

everyday.text: Whether you have a backup plan running right now: a side job, a savings cushion, a second option.

subquestions.notes: Game show seed must not read as gambling (T13B never). Frame as walking away versus one more swing.

subquestions.question: Would you trade your free time for a win people can see?
subquestions.poleA: Gives up rest and weekends for a visible result.
subquestions.poleB: Keeps the time and lets the win wait or pass.
subquestions.tension: Pushing costs rest, people and joy; easing off costs the win and maybe others' respect.

absurd.text: Genii will make you world famous at one thing of your choice, but you'll never have a lazy Sunday again.

unusual.text: A billionaire you met by accident will fund your dream project if you work from their yacht, 14-hour days, for a year.

everyday.text: The last weekend you spent working on a goal instead of resting, or chose not to.

subquestions.notes: Genii catch: no lazy Sundays (distinct from the other Genii seeds). Never read Push as greed or Easy as lazy.

subquestions.question: Does someone else's timeline set your clock?
subquestions.poleA: Measures themselves against peers and speeds up when behind.
subquestions.poleB: Ignores the race and keeps their own pace.
subquestions.tension: Comparison fuels progress but steals peace; ignoring it can mean waking up behind.

absurd.text: A glowing scoreboard appears over everyone's head showing how 'on track' their life is, and yours is lower than your roommate's.

unusual.text: At a school reunion, a former classmate hands out business cards for a company built on the idea you had first.

everyday.text: The last time you looked up where a friend or old classmate is in life, and whether you changed a plan after.

subquestions.notes: No age numbers. The reunion is fine as long as it names no age or year.

subquestions.question: Do you need to see progress, or can you trust the slow road?
subquestions.poleA: Wants milestones, numbers and proof it is working.
subquestions.poleB: Trusts the slow build and doesn't need to check.
subquestions.tension: Needing proof can kill slow good things; trusting the slow road can mean years on something that never lands.

absurd.text: You plant a magic seed that grows into anything you want, but it takes ten years and you can never check on it.

unusual.text: A master craftsperson offers you an apprenticeship: five years of sweeping the workshop before you're allowed to make anything.

everyday.text: The last skill or hobby you started: pushed it, quit it, or let it drift at your own pace.

subquestions.question: When the rule and the person conflict, which wins?
subquestions.poleA: Applies the rule the same way for everyone.
subquestions.poleB: Bends it for this person's situation.
subquestions.tension: Holding the rule can be cruel to the one; bending it can be unfair to everyone who followed it.

absurd.text: You guard a magic portal with a strict no-pets rule, and a sobbing kid arrives with a talking hamster that says it's 'basically a person'.

unusual.text: On jury duty, the evidence clearly shows the defendant stole a bakery birthday cake, for their kid's party.

everyday.text: The last time you were in charge of a rule (a deadline, a house rule, a game) and someone asked for an exception.

subquestions.notes: Jury seed: keep it tiny and warm, no crime politics, no lecture. Neither verdict option may look like the good-person answer.

subquestions.question: Is fair the same for everyone, or what each person needs?
subquestions.poleA: Equal shares, first come first served, same deal for all.
subquestions.poleB: Gives more to whoever needs it more.
subquestions.tension: Equal can ignore real need; need-based can feel like favoritism and punish whoever asked politely.

absurd.text: Genii gives you one wish to share with four friends: split it into five equal small wishes, or give the whole thing to the friend who needs it most.

unusual.text: Added by mistake to a stranger's wedding group chat, you end up running the seating chart, and three guests beg you for the good table.

everyday.text: The last time you split something among people (food, money, turns, tickets): equal shares or by need.

subquestions.notes: Genii catch: the wish is shared. Keep needs light (no health or hardship detail).

subquestions.question: Do you follow the process when nobody is checking?
subquestions.poleA: Follows it anyway; the rule is the rule even alone.
subquestions.poleB: Takes the sensible shortcut when it harms no one.
subquestions.tension: Following it can be pointless and slow; skipping it can be risky and feels unfair to the ones who waited.

absurd.text: You find a remote that pauses time for everyone but you, and the line for the new ride is four hours long.

unusual.text: You're house-sitting for a stranger with a 30-rule list, and rule 12 says: 'Never open the pantry.'

everyday.text: The last time nobody would have known if you skipped a step: a form, a line, a return.

subquestions.notes: Keep it to lines and small rules, never stealing or harm, so it is not a moral test.

subquestions.question: Is your phone an open room or a locked diary, even with the people you love?
subquestions.poleA: Hands it over unlocked without hovering.
subquestions.poleB: Keeps it locked, even with nothing to hide.
subquestions.tension: Open invites misreads of old chats and group gossip; private invites suspicion from people who love you.

absurd.text: Genii offers you an unbreakable phone with infinite battery, but its lock screen is gone forever.

unusual.text: At a party, your phone gets swapped with a coworker's identical one, and they've had yours open for an hour.

everyday.text: Whether someone other than you can unlock your phone right now.

subquestions.notes: T01B never: secretive or hiding something. The locked option needs a proud line like 'nothing to hide, still no'.

subquestions.question: When someone close asks for access, is saying no trust or distrust?
subquestions.poleA: Shares location, passcode or chats when asked.
subquestions.poleB: Declines kindly and keeps it separate.
subquestions.tension: Saying yes can make privacy feel impossible later; saying no can land as 'what are you hiding'.

absurd.text: A crystal ball appears that lets your partner see your phone screen whenever they want, and they think it's romantic.

unusual.text: A friend making a documentary about your friend group asks for everyone's old chat screenshots, and everyone else already sent theirs.

everyday.text: The last time someone close asked to see something on your phone, and what you did.

subquestions.notes: T01A never: controlling or jealous. The asker in each seed must be warm, not suspicious.

subquestions.question: Does a quiet stretch mean a friendship is fine, or fading?
subquestions.poleA: Picks up after months like no time passed.
subquestions.poleB: Notices the silence and who let it happen.
subquestions.tension: Easygoing can read as not caring; noticing can read as keeping score.

absurd.text: You wake from a magic ten-year sleep, and your phone shows exactly which friends texted you while you were out.

unusual.text: A friend you haven't talked to in two years texts 'come to my birthday in Lisbon?' like no time passed.

everyday.text: The last close friend you went months without texting, and who broke the silence.

subquestions.notes: T02B never: needy or clingy, no attachment labels. T02A never: a bad friend.

subquestions.question: Do you keep count of who reaches out first?
subquestions.poleA: Doesn't track; whoever texts, texts.
subquestions.poleB: Knows the count, and it matters more than they say.
subquestions.tension: Not counting can let one side do all the work; counting can turn a friendship into a ledger.

absurd.text: A cursed notebook fills itself with a tally of who texted first, you or each friend, and it sits open on your coffee table when people visit.

unusual.text: Your phone breaks for a whole month, and when it's fixed you see exactly who noticed you went silent.

everyday.text: Whether there's a conversation right now where you're waiting for them to text first.

subquestions.question: When feelings need words, whose words do you use?
subquestions.poleA: Lets an AI draft it, then tweaks.
subquestions.poleB: Writes it themselves, typos and all.
subquestions.tension: The AI version lands better but isn't quite you; your own version is yours but may say it badly.

absurd.text: A ghost who was a famous poet offers to write your apology to your ex in perfect prose, signed with your name.

unusual.text: Your city picks you to write the one letter that goes into its 100-year time capsule, due tomorrow.

everyday.text: The last time you wrote something that mattered (an apology, a thank-you, a message to an ex), and who or what helped.

subquestions.notes: T03A never: lonely or replacing people. T03B never: anti-tech or judgmental.

subquestions.question: When something eats at you late, who hears it first: a machine or a person?
subquestions.poleA: Types it out to an AI first.
subquestions.poleB: Tells a person, or writes it down alone.
subquestions.tension: The AI is always awake and never judges but knows nothing of you; a person knows you but might be asleep, or might judge.

absurd.text: Your houseplant starts talking back, gives great advice and never repeats anything, and your best friend is also awake.

unusual.text: Right before a long flight, your partner texts 'we need to talk when you land', and the Wi-Fi costs $30.

everyday.text: What you did the last time something was on your mind too late to call anyone.

subquestions.notes: Houseplant stands in for the AI; options must make that explicit or it scores nothing.

subquestions.question: Is your circle a fortress or an open door?
subquestions.poleA: Keeps the circle small and hard to get into.
subquestions.poleB: Lets everyone in; strangers become friends fast.
subquestions.tension: Small circles run deep but get lonely when one friend leaves; wide circles are fun but thin when you really need someone.

absurd.text: You can clone your best friend once, but after that you can never make a new friend again.

unusual.text: A two-week cruise seats you permanently at a table of six chatty strangers, or you can eat alone in your cabin.

everyday.text: The last time someone new tried to join your usual group plan, and what you did.

subquestions.notes: T04A never: snobby or cold. T04B never: fake or shallow.

subquestions.question: Do new people need to earn their way in?
subquestions.poleA: Makes people prove themselves over time.
subquestions.poleB: Introduces them to everyone tonight.
subquestions.tension: Earning keeps the circle safe but slow; opening fast risks a bad fit in the group.

absurd.text: A friendly alien lands in your backyard and asks to meet all your friends tonight.

unusual.text: Your new neighbor knocks with homemade bread and asks to join your friend group's standing Thursday dinner.

everyday.text: The last follow request from someone you had met exactly once.

subquestions.question: Do you show love by doing or by saying?
subquestions.poleA: Shows up and does the thing, quietly.
subquestions.poleB: Says it, writes it, makes it explicit.
subquestions.tension: Doing can go unnoticed or unthanked; saying can feel cheap if nothing follows.

absurd.text: A spell makes you choose for one year: you can never say a kind word to your friends, or you can never do them a favor.

unusual.text: Your friend wins a local award: you get 60 seconds at the mic, or a free afternoon to secretly clean their messy apartment.

everyday.text: The last time a friend had a rough week: whether you did something or said something.

subquestions.notes: T05A never: rude. T05B never: all talk.

subquestions.question: Would you rather show up grumbling, or send love from a distance?
subquestions.poleA: Goes in person and complains the whole way.
subquestions.poleB: Stays away and sends something heartfelt.
subquestions.tension: Showing up grumpy can sour the help; love from afar can feel like skipping out.

absurd.text: A dragon kidnaps your friend's cat, and you can fight it yourself, badly, or write the dragon a very persuasive letter.

unusual.text: Your friend moves into a fourth-floor walk-up in a snowstorm, on your one free Saturday this month.

everyday.text: The last time someone you know moved house: whether you carried boxes, or sent something instead.

subquestions.question: When a friend needs you and you're running on empty, who wins?
subquestions.poleA: Shows up anyway, running on fumes.
subquestions.poleB: Protects the battery and checks in later.
subquestions.tension: Showing up empty can make you resentful and less useful; protecting yourself can leave a friend alone when it counted.

absurd.text: Your social battery appears as a number above your head, it's at 2%, and your friend's crisis needs 20%.

unusual.text: Your friend's first-ever stand-up set is tonight, and you've just walked in from a 12-hour shift.

everyday.text: The last time you'd planned to rest and a friend asked for something.

subquestions.notes: Capacity only: score the tag, never R2 (library rule). T06B never: selfish; T06A never: a pushover.

subquestions.question: Do your own rules (budget, bedtime, plans) bend for a friend?
subquestions.poleA: Breaks their own rule for the friend.
subquestions.poleB: Keeps the rule, joins another way.
subquestions.tension: Bending can drain money and sleep for weeks; holding firm can make you the one who's never there.

absurd.text: Your best friend turns into a vampire and can only hang out at night, and your job starts at 7am.

unusual.text: A friend wins a resort trip for two and picks you, but it's next week and flights aren't included.

everyday.text: The last time a friend's plan cost more money or hours than you'd planned to give.

subquestions.notes: T06B never: not having the money. Keep money pressure out of options or mark it circumstance.

subquestions.question: When a friend asks for the real answer, do you give it raw or wrapped?
subquestions.poleA: Gives it straight, no cushion.
subquestions.poleB: Wraps it so it lands, even if slower.
subquestions.tension: Raw can hurt more than it helps; wrapped can blur the message until it's missed.

absurd.text: Your friend's goldfish, which has predicted everything correctly for a year, tells only you that their new business will flop; they sign the lease tomorrow.

unusual.text: Your friend is proposing tonight and asks what you really think of their partner.

everyday.text: The last time a friend was clearly in the wrong with someone and asked you to back them.

subquestions.notes: Goldfish works only if the prediction is trusted; say so in the hook. Proposal seed: intimate privacy.

subquestions.question: Do you tell a friend what everyone else is saying about them?
subquestions.poleA: Tells them straight.
subquestions.poleB: Shields them, hints, or softens it.
subquestions.tension: Telling can crush them and burn your sources; shielding lets them keep embarrassing themselves.

absurd.text: For one night you can hear what everyone at a party thinks, and the whole room thinks your friend's new band is a disaster.

unusual.text: At a work party, you overhear the boss say your friend won't get the promotion they're counting on.

everyday.text: The last time you knew something unflattering about a friend that they didn't know.

subquestions.notes: Never about looks or bodies. T07A never: rude; T07B never: dishonest.

subquestions.question: Can someone who hurt you get back in?
subquestions.poleA: Opens the door again.
subquestions.poleB: Forgives on paper, keeps the door on the chain.
subquestions.tension: Opening again risks the same hurt twice; staying guarded can end something that could have healed.

absurd.text: A witch turns the friend who betrayed you into a puppy until someone forgives them, and the puppy is at your door.

unusual.text: Stuck in an elevator for two hours with your ex, who uses the time to apologize, properly.

everyday.text: The last person who let you down twice, and what you said on the third ask.

subquestions.notes: Puppy seed: forgiving a puppy is too easy. Options must keep the stakes real (forgiveness turns them back and back into the group chat).

subquestions.question: Do you forgive and forget, or forgive and file?
subquestions.poleA: Lets the memory go with the grudge.
subquestions.poleB: Forgives and keeps the record.
subquestions.tension: Forgetting leaves you open to a repeat; keeping the file keeps the old hurt alive.

absurd.text: A magic eraser can wipe your memory of every wrong a friend ever did to you: the friendship stays, the memories go.

unusual.text: The friend who ghosted you for a year shows up on Monday as your new team lead.

everyday.text: I bet you have a screenshot saved 'just in case' of something someone said.

subquestions.notes: T08B never: vindictive or petty as a flaw. The eraser 'no' option must read as wise, not bitter.

subquestions.question: When you're in love, does your life fold into theirs?
subquestions.poleA: Their day becomes your day; plans, friends and hobbies merge.
subquestions.poleB: Keeps own plans, friends and weekends intact.
subquestions.tension: Folding in feels close but can erase you; staying separate can make your partner feel like a guest.

absurd.text: A spell merges your and your partner's friend groups, playlists and hobbies into one, and neither of you remembers whose were whose.

unusual.text: Your partner lands a year-long job abroad and asks you to come, leaving your job, friends and your weekly thing.

everyday.text: The last weekend your partner had plans without you, and what you did with yours.

subquestions.notes: T09A never: clingy, no gendered read. T09B never: avoidant. Intimate privacy for the abroad seed.

subquestions.question: In love, do you keep something that's only yours?
subquestions.poleA: Wants to share every hobby and night.
subquestions.poleB: Keeps a hobby, a friend or a night just for them.
subquestions.tension: Sharing everything can smother; keeping a corner can feel like shutting them out.

absurd.text: Your partner drinks a potion that makes them instantly world-class at your solo hobby, and now they want to come every time.

unusual.text: Your partner signs you both up for a couples' cooking class every Thursday, the only night you have your own thing.

everyday.text: Whether you have a hobby, friend or night right now that's yours alone.

subquestions.question: When a relationship gets rocky, do you repair it or release it?
subquestions.poleA: Sits down and fixes it.
subquestions.poleB: Lets it end, quietly and kindly.
subquestions.tension: Repairing can mean years in something that should have ended; releasing can mean losing something one talk could have saved.

absurd.text: A repair shop for friendships opens next door: any friendship fixed, but you both sit inside together until it's done, however long it takes.

unusual.text: On a two-week road trip, you and your travel buddy stop speaking on day three, with eleven days left.

everyday.text: The last friendship that faded, and whether you tried to fix it or let it drift.

subquestions.notes: Applies to any relationship (friend, roommate, person). T10A never: a doormat.

subquestions.question: Does ending something need a conversation?
subquestions.poleA: Says it out loud, face to face.
subquestions.poleB: Lets it fade with fewer plans.
subquestions.tension: The talk is painful and can turn into a fight; the fade leaves the other person guessing.

absurd.text: You and a friend wear cursed matching rings that only come off when one of you says 'it's over' to the other's face.

unusual.text: Your band has been dying for months, and the group chat vote on whether to keep going is tomorrow.

everyday.text: The last group, club or plan you stopped showing up to, and whether you said anything.

subquestions.notes: Keep 'band' swappable (team, book club) for variety across cards.

subquestions.question: Is raising a kid part of the life you picture?
subquestions.poleA: Pictures raising a kid and wants it.
subquestions.poleB: Pictures a full life without one.
subquestions.tension: Wanting it means trading freedom and years; not wanting it means answering the same question at every family dinner.

absurd.text: A stork drops off a perfectly behaved baby dragon that needs a home for 18 years; keep it or fly it back.

unusual.text: You're the only one free to look after a friend's three kids for a whole weekend, and the kids adore you.

everyday.text: The last time a friend's kid fell asleep on you or wouldn't stop playing with you, and your first thought.

subquestions.notes: Library marks T11 locked18; spec 21 says no age gates, so write for anyone and mark privacy intimate. Dragon seed maps weakly unless options speak of the life (18 years of raising someone) rather than the pet. T11B never: hating kids.

subquestions.question: Would you trade freedom for a family, or a family for freedom?
subquestions.poleA: Chooses the family life.
subquestions.poleB: Chooses the free life.
subquestions.tension: Family costs freedom and time; freedom can cost the future you once pictured.

absurd.text: Genii lets you peek ten seconds into two futures: a loud kitchen full of kids, or a passport full of stamps; you have to pick one to keep.

unusual.text: Your partner wins a paid year off and asks: a see-the-world year, or a start-a-family year?

everyday.text: I bet you've already picked out names for a future kid, pet or boat.

subquestions.notes: Genii catch: a ten-second peek, pick one. Never frame the free life as selfish.

subquestions.question: Is fair paying the same, or feeling it the same?
subquestions.poleA: Splits exactly 50/50, whatever each earns.
subquestions.poleB: Splits by what each has, so it pinches the same.
subquestions.tension: Even splits can squeeze the one who earns less; income splits can feel like charity or a debt.

absurd.text: Your new housemate is a mermaid with a sunken-ship fortune who insists on splitting the rent exactly 50/50.

unusual.text: Right after you move in together, your partner gets a surprise promotion that triples their pay.

everyday.text: The last group dinner where you'd ordered much less than everyone else and the bill came.

subquestions.notes: Mermaid seed needs one side richer; keep it the other person so the player isn't the rich one. T12A never: stingy.

subquestions.question: Do you keep a tab with the people you love?
subquestions.poleA: Tracks every debt and pays back exactly.
subquestions.poleB: Keeps it loose; whoever has it pays.
subquestions.tension: Tracking can make love feel like an invoice; keeping it loose can let one person quietly carry everyone.

absurd.text: A cursed ledger makes every debt between you and your friends glow on their foreheads until it's settled.

unusual.text: You win a free week in a villa for six, and your friends ask how you'll split groceries and the cleaning fee.

everyday.text: Whether someone owes you money right now, and whether you know the exact amount.

subquestions.question: Found money: joy now, or cushion later?
subquestions.poleA: Spends it on something memorable, now.
subquestions.poleB: Saves it.
subquestions.tension: Spending now can leave you short later; saving can mean a life that's always on hold.

absurd.text: A leprechaun gives you a pot of gold that doubles every year you don't touch it and vanishes the moment you do.

unusual.text: You return a stranger's lost wallet and they hand you $1,000 cash on the spot.

everyday.text: What happened to the last money you didn't expect: a refund, a gift, cash in an old pocket.

subquestions.notes: T13A never: reckless or gambling. T13B never: boring or cheap.

subquestions.question: Do you book it before you can afford it?
subquestions.poleA: Books the thing first and figures out money after.
subquestions.poleB: Checks the balance first, every time.
subquestions.tension: Booking first makes great stories and scary bank weeks; checking first means some shows go on without you.

absurd.text: A time traveler offers a one-way ticket to any concert in history, tonight, for your whole savings.

unusual.text: Your favorite artist announces a secret show in a castle abroad; tickets drop in ten minutes and flights cost a month's rent.

everyday.text: I bet you've booked something before checking your balance.

subquestions.question: Is owning the thing you love worth paying extra?
subquestions.poleA: Pays more for the one they love.
subquestions.poleB: Walks away happy with less or nothing.
subquestions.tension: Buying the nice one costs money and space; skipping it can mean living with things you only half like.

absurd.text: A cursed store lets you take anything you want, free, but everything you already own disappears.

unusual.text: An auction house mistakes you for a bidder, and you have 30 seconds to bid on the one object you've wanted for years.

everyday.text: The last time you bought one more of something you already had plenty of.

subquestions.notes: T14A never: vain or shallow. T14B never: cheap or joyless.

subquestions.question: Does less stuff feel like freedom or like loss?
subquestions.poleA: Holds on; things carry meaning.
subquestions.poleB: Clears out; empty shelves feel good.
subquestions.tension: Keeping clutters your space and life; clearing can throw out memories you'll miss.

absurd.text: A friendly tornado offers to take every object you own and leave behind one perfect thing of your choice.

unusual.text: You win a tiny house, but everything you own has to fit inside 20 square meters by Friday.

everyday.text: Whether you've cleared out or given away a bag of stuff in the last three months.

subquestions.question: When someone succeeds, do you see the effort or the head start?
subquestions.poleA: Sees the effort and gives full credit.
subquestions.poleB: Spots the head start and says so.
subquestions.tension: Crediting effort can ignore unfair starts; naming the head start can sound bitter.

absurd.text: A fairy godparent makes your friend famous overnight, and in every interview they say they 'grinded for years'.

unusual.text: On a podcast, a friend whose parents bought their apartment gets called 'self-made' and doesn't correct the host.

everyday.text: The last time someone's big win came up in conversation, and your first thought.

subquestions.notes: Never political or about groups of people; always one specific friend. T15A never: looking down on people who struggle. T15B never: envious or bitter.

subquestions.question: Should the reward go to whoever worked hardest, or be shared?
subquestions.poleA: Bigger share to whoever did more.
subquestions.poleB: Equal shares; luck and help count too.
subquestions.tension: Merit shares feel fair to the hard worker and cold to everyone else; equal shares feel warm and quietly unfair.

absurd.text: You and a friend find a treasure chest: you did all the digging, they had the lucky map.

unusual.text: Your group wins a $10,000 trivia championship, and one friend answered 80% of the questions.

everyday.text: The last group project or team win, and whether you wanted credit split by who did what.

subquestions.question: Is work a race to win or a job that ends when it ends?
subquestions.poleA: Gives extra time for the visible win.
subquestions.poleB: Logs off; life starts after work.
subquestions.tension: Racing costs rest and people; logging off can cost the promotion and the title.

absurd.text: A cursed watch gives you one extra hour of genius every day, but only if you spend it working.

unusual.text: Your boss's boss offers you the top job, but it comes with a phone that stays on, even on vacation.

everyday.text: Whether you checked work or school messages last weekend.

subquestions.notes: T16A never: workaholic or greedy. T16B never: lazy.

subquestions.question: Do you keep a quiet tally of your wins?
subquestions.poleA: Knows the count and wants it seen.
subquestions.poleB: Barely notices; moves on.
subquestions.tension: Tallying drives you and makes others feel judged; not tallying can mean nobody notices your work, including you.

absurd.text: A magic shelf appears in your room that fills with a trophy for every win you've ever had, and your friends can see it.

unusual.text: You're nominated for a public award alongside your best friend, and only one of you can win.

everyday.text: The last win you had, and how soon after it you told someone.

subquestions.question: Would you rather know the ending, or keep the surprise?
subquestions.poleA: Wants it decided, booked, known.
subquestions.poleB: Keeps it open; not knowing is fine.
subquestions.tension: Knowing brings calm and kills surprise; not knowing keeps doors open and keeps you up at night.

absurd.text: A fortune cookie will tell you exactly where you'll live, what you'll do and who you'll be with in ten years, in one bite.

unusual.text: A perfect job offer needs an answer within one hour, and your dream interview is next week.

everyday.text: The last big plan you left undecided, and how long before you locked it in.

subquestions.notes: T17A never: anxious or 'behind'. T17B never: lost or flaky.

subquestions.question: Does an open question calm you or keep you up?
subquestions.poleA: Signs the long deal to feel settled.
subquestions.poleB: Keeps it month to month.
subquestions.tension: Locking in trades freedom for calm; staying open trades calm for freedom.

absurd.text: You wake up holding a magic contract that locks in your entire next five years, good ones, and you can sign it or tear it.

unusual.text: Your landlord offers a five-year lease at a great price, or month-to-month for more.

everyday.text: Whether you have something booked more than six months out right now.

subquestions.question: When family needs help, are you the first name they call?
subquestions.poleA: Says 'I've got it' before anyone else answers.
subquestions.poleB: Helps, and shares the load or sets the terms.
subquestions.tension: Being first can wear you down and let siblings coast; setting limits can hurt family feelings and bring guilt.

absurd.text: Your whole family gets shrunk to the size of mice, and only you, still full size, can look after them for a year of weekends.

unusual.text: A relative's bakery is about to close, and they ask you to run it for six months, unpaid.

everyday.text: The last time someone in your family asked for help, and how fast you said yes.

subquestions.notes: No care-giving for illness. T18A never: a martyr. T18B never: cold.

subquestions.question: Where does family help end, and who decides?
subquestions.poleA: Keeps helping; family is family.
subquestions.poleB: Names an end date or a limit.
subquestions.tension: No limits can drain you for years; limits can feel like abandoning someone you love.

absurd.text: You gave your sibling a magic wishing coin; they've used it 47 times this month and now ask for the 48th.

unusual.text: Your adult sibling moved onto your couch 'for two weeks', and it's now month five.

everyday.text: The last time you said no, or set a limit, with a family member.

subquestions.question: Does your family get a vote on your big choices?
subquestions.poleA: Decides alone and tells them after.
subquestions.poleB: Asks them first and weighs their view.
subquestions.tension: Deciding alone can hurt them and cost support; giving a vote can mean living their plan.

absurd.text: A magic family portrait in your hallway frowns or smiles at every decision you make, and every guest can see it.

unusual.text: You get into a dream program on the other side of the world, and your family calls a video meeting about it before you've said yes.

everyday.text: The last big decision you made, and whether your family heard before or after.

subquestions.notes: T19A never: ungrateful. T19B never: a pushover.

subquestions.question: When your family says 'absolutely not', what do you do?
subquestions.poleA: Does it anyway and tells them later.
subquestions.poleB: Negotiates, sends an ally, or drops it for peace.
subquestions.tension: Going ahead can split the family; dropping it can mean a dream you never try.

absurd.text: Your family bakes your passport into a cake to stop you running off to join the circus.

unusual.text: Your family finds out from a cousin's post that you've already quit your job to open a food truck.

everyday.text: The last time your family said no to a plan of yours, and what you did.

subquestions.question: Should your home run the way homes 'should'?
subquestions.poleA: Runs it the classic way.
subquestions.poleB: Invents the rules as they go.
subquestions.tension: Classic can mean living roles that don't fit you; your own way can mean friction with family and constant negotiation.

absurd.text: You're given a free lighthouse to live in, but it comes with the old keeper's 300-year household rulebook.

unusual.text: Your partner's family gives you both a thick 'how our family runs a home' binder at the housewarming.

everyday.text: Whether chores at your place now split the way they did in the home you grew up in.

subquestions.notes: T20A never: old-fashioned. T20B never: disrespectful to family. Gender neutral roles only.

subquestions.question: Are traditions to keep, remix, or retire?
subquestions.poleA: Keeps them as they are.
subquestions.poleB: Remixes or retires them.
subquestions.tension: Keeping can feel empty if the meaning is gone; changing can hurt the people who built them.

absurd.text: You can erase one family tradition forever, or invent a new one that everyone must follow for 100 years.

unusual.text: You end up hosting the big family holiday for the first time because the usual host is abroad.

everyday.text: The last holiday or birthday you celebrated your own way instead of the usual way.

subquestions.notes: No religion; say 'holiday' only.

subquestions.question: Does love need a big public 'yes'?
subquestions.poleA: Wants the big official moment.
subquestions.poleB: Doesn't need the stamp.
subquestions.tension: The big moment costs money and stress; skipping it can hurt family who dreamed of it.

absurd.text: A magic skywriter offers to announce your commitment in the clouds over the whole city, including over your ex's building.

unusual.text: You win a free wedding in a raffle, full traditional package, valid only this year.

everyday.text: Whether you've ever saved a wedding idea somewhere: a screenshot, a board, a note.

subquestions.notes: Library marks T21 locked18; write for anyone, allow 'not my life'. T21B never: against marriage for others. Intimate privacy.

subquestions.question: Who belongs at the big moments: everyone, or just us?
subquestions.poleA: Every relative, the more the better.
subquestions.poleB: Just the two of them, or a few.
subquestions.tension: Everyone means a day that belongs to the family; just us means some people will feel left out forever.

absurd.text: A giant friendly whale offers to carry just you and your partner to a secret island, or all 300 of your relatives to a party on its back.

unusual.text: Your family starts a group chat called 'THE WEDDING' before you've even decided to get married.

everyday.text: Your last big celebration (a birthday, a graduation, a move), and how many people were there.

subquestions.notes: Everyday seed keeps this answerable for people with no wedding plans.

subquestions.question: The new thing or your thing?
subquestions.poleA: Picks the thing nobody has tried.
subquestions.poleB: Picks the one they know they love.
subquestions.tension: New can disappoint; your thing can mean never finding something better.

absurd.text: Your fridge restocks itself every morning with either your all-time favorite meal or a random dish from somewhere in the world; you choose which, forever.

unusual.text: On a work trip abroad with one free day, you can go back to the café you loved last time, or ride a random bus to the end of the line.

everyday.text: The last time you ordered at your usual place: the usual, or something new.

subquestions.notes: Food as taste only; never diet. T22A never: restless. T22B never: boring.

subquestions.question: Is a routine a comfort or a cage?
subquestions.poleA: Would take the random days, good or bad.
subquestions.poleB: Would take the same good day on repeat.
subquestions.tension: Routine is safe and can go stale; randomness is alive and can go badly.

absurd.text: You can live the same perfect day on repeat forever, or live random days that could be better or worse.

unusual.text: A stranger on a train offers to swap lives with you for one week: home, job and routine included.

everyday.text: How many times you've rewatched your comfort show.

subquestions.question: Whose is your free time?
subquestions.poleA: Gives it to whoever needs help.
subquestions.poleB: Keeps it for their own thing.
subquestions.tension: Giving it away can leave nothing for you; keeping it can mean people stop asking.

absurd.text: A village of tiny gnomes asks you to help rebuild their town every Saturday for a year, and they pay in pastries.

unusual.text: An animal shelter's big adoption day loses half its volunteers that morning, on your one free Saturday.

everyday.text: What you did with your last fully free afternoon.

subquestions.notes: T23A never: morally better. T23B never: selfish.

subquestions.question: Do you put your shoes on when someone says they need hands?
subquestions.poleA: Is already moving before the ask is done.
subquestions.poleB: Waits to see if someone else goes.
subquestions.tension: Always going gets you used; waiting gets you seen as the one who never comes.

absurd.text: Anyone in the world can summon you with a whistle when they need help; you can switch it off, but they'll all know.

unusual.text: Your building's group chat asks who can help carry a piano up five flights, right now.

everyday.text: The last time someone in a group said 'I need a hand', and how fast you moved.

subquestions.question: Do you run your life by numbers or by feel?
subquestions.poleA: Tracks it: budgets, calendars, lists.
subquestions.poleB: Knows how it's going by how it feels.
subquestions.tension: Tracking can become a second job; going by feel can let things slip until they hurt.

absurd.text: A talking calculator follows you around for a week, saying the exact numbers of your day out loud.

unusual.text: You're throwing a surprise party for 40 people, and the one rule is no lists, only your memory.

everyday.text: Whether you could say, within five dollars, what you spent on fun last month.

subquestions.notes: T24A never: obsessive. T24B never: chaotic.

subquestions.question: Does a plan calm you or cage you?
subquestions.poleA: Wants the schedule.
subquestions.poleB: Wants the day open.
subquestions.tension: A schedule brings calm and kills spontaneity; an open day brings freedom and forgotten things.

absurd.text: A wizard offers to schedule the next year of your life perfectly, down to the snack breaks.

unusual.text: Snowed into a mountain lodge for four days with strangers, one of them proposes a strict group schedule.

everyday.text: How many alarms, lists or calendars you have running right now.

subquestions.question: In a game, is a rule a rule?
subquestions.poleA: Plays by the rulebook.
subquestions.poleB: Lets it slide for fun or for the person.
subquestions.tension: Strict play can kill the fun; bending can make the game meaningless for everyone else.

absurd.text: You referee a match between two teams of kittens, and the tiniest kitten keeps accidentally cheating.

unusual.text: At a charity board game tournament, your partner quietly offers to peek at the answer cards.

everyday.text: The last time someone bent the rules in a game you were playing.

subquestions.notes: T25A never: rigid or a snitch. T25B never: unfair.

subquestions.question: Does fair mean first come, first served, or the right call for each case?
subquestions.poleA: Honors the booking, the queue, the first to ask.
subquestions.poleB: Helps whoever needs it most right now.
subquestions.tension: The queue can feel cold; the exception can feel unfair to whoever followed the rules.

absurd.text: In a blizzard you run the only warm barn: 60 chickens need in, but 60 chocolate chip muffins for tomorrow's fair booked the space first.

unusual.text: Checking tickets at a sold-out show, you face a crying fan holding a ticket for last night.

everyday.text: The last time you were in line and someone asked to go ahead of you.

subquestions.notes: Founder's chickens and muffins seed. It works only because the muffins booked first: the booking is the rule, the chickens are the need. Keep that in the hook or the card is a joke with no evidence.
